seoTitle: How to Short in TradingView Paper Trading
metaDescription: Learn how to enable TradingView Paper Trading, place a short order step by step, and set stop loss and take profit without risking real money.
intro: Practicing a short trade without putting real money on the line is exactly what TradingView's Paper Trading feature is built for. This guide covers enabling paper trading, placing a short order, and managing stop loss and take profit levels on a simulated position.

steps.heading: Understand short selling
steps.body: Short selling means opening a position that profits when the price falls, betting against the asset rather than on it rising.

steps.heading: Enable Paper Trading
steps.body: Turn on TradingView's Paper Trading panel to get a simulated account balance you can trade with risk-free.

steps.heading: Place a short order
steps.body: From the paper trading panel, select sell/short instead of buy, choose your position size, and submit the order on your chosen symbol.

steps.heading: Set stop loss and take profit
steps.body: Add a stop loss above your entry to limit downside if the price rises, and a take profit below your entry to lock in gains if the price falls as expected.

steps.heading: Close or modify the position
steps.body: Monitor the simulated trade and close it manually or let your stop loss/take profit orders execute automatically once conditions are met.

faq.question: Is TradingView Paper Trading free?
faq.answer: Yes, Paper Trading is included as a free simulated trading feature on TradingView.

faq.question: Can I practice short selling on crypto and stocks in paper trading?
faq.answer: Yes, Paper Trading supports short positions across the asset classes available on TradingView's connected paper trading brokers.

faq.question: Does paper trading use real market prices?
faq.answer: Yes, paper trading uses live or delayed real market data, so your simulated trades reflect actual price movement.

faq.question: What happens if I don't set a stop loss on a short trade?
faq.answer: Without a stop loss, a simulated short position can accumulate unlimited paper losses if the price keeps rising, so it's good practice to always set one.
